topics.name: Photosynthesis
topics.summary: How green plants build their own food from light, water and carbon dioxide, and what limits the rate.

topics.name: Genetics and Inheritance

objectives.text: State the word and balanced equations for photosynthesis.
Explain the role of chlorophyll, light, water and carbon dioxide.
Describe the limiting factors that control the rate.

keyTerms.definition: The process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy.
The organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.
Small pores, mostly on the underside of a leaf, that let gases in and out.
The factor in shortest supply, which alone caps the rate of a process.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Photosynthesis is how nearly all food on Earth begins. You will learn what goes in, what comes out, where in the leaf it happens, and what controls how fast it runs.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
Animals eat. Plants cannot — so they build their own food instead, out of air, water and sunlight.

This matters beyond botany. Every animal either eats plants or eats something that ate plants, and the oxygen you are breathing right now was released by photosynthesis. It is the entry point of energy into almost every food chain.

sections.heading: The equation
sections.body:
In words:

    carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
                (in the presence of light and chlorophyll)

Balanced:

    6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

Read what this says. The plant takes two low-energy substances and builds one high-energy one. Light supplies the energy for that; chlorophyll captures the light. Neither is consumed as a raw material, which is why both are written above the arrow rather than in it.

Oxygen is a by-product. The plant does not make it deliberately — it is simply left over.

sections.heading: Where it happens
sections.body:
Photosynthesis occurs in CHLOROPLASTS, concentrated in the palisade layer near the upper surface of the leaf where light is strongest.

A leaf is well built for the job:
• Broad and flat — large surface area for catching light.
• Thin — gases diffuse across a short distance.
• Stomata on the underside — let CO₂ in and O₂ out.
• Veins — deliver water from the roots, carry glucose away.

Each feature is a solution to a supply problem: light, gas, water or transport.

sections.heading: Limiting factors
sections.body:
Three things control the rate, and at any moment ONE of them is holding the process back — whichever is in shortest supply. That one is the limiting factor.

• LIGHT INTENSITY — more light, faster rate, until another factor takes over.
• CARBON DIOXIDE CONCENTRATION — usually the limiting factor outdoors, since air is only about 0.04% CO₂.
• TEMPERATURE — raises the rate up to an optimum, then the rate falls sharply as enzymes denature.

The temperature curve behaves differently from the other two, and examiners like this point. Light and CO₂ level off at a plateau. Temperature rises, peaks, then DROPS — because enzymes are proteins and heat destroys their shape permanently.
sections.example:
Interpreting a rate-against-light-intensity graph:

The steep early section — light is limiting. Adding light adds rate.

The flat plateau — light is no longer limiting. Something else (CO₂ or temperature) has become the cap, so extra light changes nothing.

Exam technique: if a graph plateaus, do not answer "the plant has enough light". Say which factor has BECOME limiting instead.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. Write the balanced equation from memory, then check it.
2. A farmer grows tomatoes in a greenhouse and adds CO₂ to the air. Why might this increase yield — and when would it make no difference at all?
3. Explain why a plant kept in constant darkness dies even though it still has water and CO₂.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂, requiring light and chlorophyll.
• It happens in chloroplasts, mainly in the palisade layer.
• Leaf structure solves the supply problems of light, gas and water.
• Light, CO₂ and temperature can each limit the rate.
• Only temperature causes the rate to FALL past the optimum, because enzymes denature.

objectives.text: Distinguish gene, allele, genotype and phenotype.
Complete a Punnett square and state the expected ratio.

keyTerms.definition: A length of DNA coding for one characteristic.
A version of a gene. You inherit one from each parent.
The alleles an organism carries, e.g. Tt.
The characteristic actually shown, e.g. tall.

sections.heading: What you will learn
sections.body: Why children resemble their parents without being identical to them — and how to predict, with real numbers, what a cross will produce.

sections.heading: The vocabulary matters
sections.body:
Genetics questions are lost on vocabulary more than on reasoning, so be precise:

A GENE is the instruction for a characteristic — say, height in a pea plant.
An ALLELE is a version of that instruction — tall, or short.

You carry two alleles for each gene: one from each parent. Together they are your GENOTYPE. What you actually look like is your PHENOTYPE.

The distinction is the whole subject in miniature: two organisms can look identical and carry different alleles. TT and Tt are both tall, but they do not breed the same way.

sections.heading: Dominant and recessive
sections.body:
A DOMINANT allele shows in the phenotype whenever it is present, even in a single copy. Capital letter: T.

A RECESSIVE allele shows ONLY when no dominant allele is present — so both must be recessive. Lower case: t.

    TT → tall
    Tt → tall   (the T masks the t)
    tt → short

So short plants have exactly one possible genotype, tt. A tall plant could be TT or Tt, and you cannot tell by looking. Use the SAME letter in both cases — T and t, never T and s.

sections.heading: The Punnett square
sections.body:
A Punnett square sets out every way the parents’ alleles can combine.

Cross two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt). Each parent passes on either T or t:

            T       t
        ┌───────┬───────┐
    T   │  TT   │  Tt   │
        ├───────┼───────┤
    t   │  Tt   │  tt   │
        └───────┴───────┘

Four equally likely outcomes: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.

Genotype ratio  1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt
Phenotype ratio 3 tall : 1 short

That 3:1 is the signature of a monohybrid cross between two heterozygotes. Recognising it in a question is often the fastest route to the answer.
sections.example:
A different cross: Tt × tt.

            t       t
        ┌───────┬───────┐
    T   │  Tt   │  Tt   │
        ├───────┼───────┤
    t   │  tt   │  tt   │
        └───────┴───────┘

Genotype ratio  2 Tt : 2 tt  →  1 : 1
Phenotype ratio 1 tall : 1 short

Half the offspring are short here, where the Tt × Tt cross gave only a quarter. Same alleles, different ratio — which is why you must draw the square rather than recall "3:1" by reflex.

sections.heading: Probability, not prophecy
sections.body:
A 3:1 ratio does NOT promise that four offspring will be exactly three tall and one short. It is a probability: each offspring independently has a 3-in-4 chance of being tall.

With four seeds you might well get four tall ones. With four hundred, the proportion will sit close to 3:1. Large numbers are what make the ratio visible — a point worth stating explicitly when a question asks you to interpret unexpected results.

sections.heading: Try it yourself
sections.body:
1. In pea plants, purple flowers (P) are dominant to white (p). Cross Pp × Pp. Give both ratios.
2. A white-flowered plant is crossed with a purple one and half the offspring are white. What was the purple parent’s genotype?
3. Explain why two brown-eyed parents can have a blue-eyed child.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.body:
• Gene = instruction, allele = version, genotype = alleles carried, phenotype = appearance.
• Dominant shows with one copy; recessive needs two.
• Use one letter, capital for dominant and lower case for recessive.
• Tt × Tt gives 3:1; Tt × tt gives 1:1. Draw the square rather than recalling a ratio.
• Ratios are probabilities and show themselves reliably only in large numbers.

questions.question: Which are the raw materials for photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: The equation is 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Carbon dioxide and water go in; glucose and oxygen come out. Glucose and oxygen are the PRODUCTS — reversing them is the most common slip, and it describes respiration instead.

questions.question: Why is chlorophyll written above the arrow in the equation rather than as a reactant?
options: It is used up during the reaction
It absorbs light energy but is not consumed
It is a product of the reaction
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll captures light energy so the reaction can proceed, but it is not used up and does not end up in the glucose. The same is true of light itself. Substances written above the arrow enable the reaction without being consumed by it.

questions.question: A graph of photosynthesis rate against light intensity rises then levels off. What does the flat section show?
options: Light is still the limiting factor
Another factor, such as CO₂ or temperature, has become limiting
The chlorophyll has been used up
questions.explanation: While the line rises, light is limiting — more light gives more rate. Once it plateaus, adding light changes nothing, so something else is now the constraint, usually CO₂ concentration or temperature. The plant is still photosynthesising, just capped by a different factor. Answering "it has enough light" does not name the limiting factor and loses marks.

questions.question: Unlike light intensity, raising temperature well past the optimum makes the rate FALL. Why?
options: Enzymes denature and lose their shape
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is enzyme-controlled, and enzymes are proteins. Excess heat changes the shape of the active site permanently, so reactions slow sharply. This is why the temperature curve peaks and falls, while light and CO₂ curves simply level off — a distinction examiners test often.

questions.question: What is the difference between genotype and phenotype?
options: Genotype is the alleles carried; phenotype is the characteristic shown
Genotype is what you see; phenotype is the DNA
Genotype applies to plants, phenotype to animals
questions.explanation: Genotype is the pair of alleles an organism carries, such as Tt. Phenotype is the characteristic that results, such as "tall". The distinction matters because TT and Tt give the same phenotype but behave differently when bred.

questions.question: Crossing two heterozygous plants (Tt × Tt) gives what phenotype ratio?
questions.explanation: The Punnett square gives TT, Tt, Tt and tt. The first three all contain at least one dominant T, so they are tall; only tt is short. That is 3 tall : 1 short. The genotype ratio is different — 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt — so read carefully which ratio the question wants.

questions.question: A tall plant crossed with a short plant (tt) produces about half tall and half short offspring. What is the tall parent’s genotype?
questions.explanation: If the tall parent were TT, every offspring would inherit a T and all would be tall. Getting roughly half short means the tall parent must carry a recessive allele to pass on, so it is Tt. Tt × tt gives a 1:1 ratio, which is exactly what was observed.
